legacy-32681ec7100d7432ee9b384e8d0d11bac.value: Asantehene and state council with component chiefly autonomy

legacy-306a7adcf40a3a49efa62dda927986bf0.value: Polity distinguished from Asante people; no exact territorial extent or early ruler chronology inferred.

legacy-3897f0b6864abda109927b12cd8a46f52.value: Awadh — Saadat Ali Khan’s Nawabi government

legacy-c182018c10397433d35f603b75e5786f8.value: Saadat Ali Khan’s documented Nawabi tenure includes this narrow interval. Treaty dependency, the 1801 territorial changes and later royal elevation remain research gaps; the Lucknow patronage account is not used to claim unrestricted sovereignty.

legacy-b0c787592ac098eaac7da1cdeee0751b1.value: Early kingdom frame; later British conquests are outside these bounds.

legacy-fc72b8fb1572f3a036868519110eb4e86.value: Bangkok dynastic frame ends at the 1932 coup; suzerainty is not modern territorial sovereignty.

legacy-59f44c4f94d4e25b29d4c07ad702baaa0.value: Kingdom of Kaarta — early nineteenth century

legacy-3cf322aa79217816c3ab2755a109789a4.value: Kaarta retained a political identity distinct from Segu; no nineteenth-century successor, capital or detailed dynasty projected from sparse chronology.

legacy-ada893537ea0d3976d4af4c45ec318552.value: Kingdom of Segu — early nineteenth century

legacy-d91fb7b5c9bbaa3d8fd235f5d6423a7fa.value: One-year editorial partial of the documented kingdom; disputed or erroneous 1818 conquest shorthand is excluded.

legacy-cd340743ad1be907194758874ad326807.value: Sultanate with historically variable tributary relations

legacy-070411c76422c15b820b36fddc83b7e24.value: Bagirmi had court and administrative institutions; tributary dependence changed between larger neighbours. Exact 1800 overlordship and territorial extent are not independently fixed here.

legacy-7ee20559d94a35b027c87fff830b1e946.value: The Darfur sultans governed through royal court institutions and contested elite influence. This is a historical political framework, not automatic identification of every Fur community or the modern geographic region as sovereign.

legacy-8eee4734724f604979158a6929b0359a6.value: This partial 1800 core precedes the 1808 Fulani capture of Ngazargamu and subsequent redistribution of political authority. Tribute ties and broad labels are not uniform sovereignty over all geometry.

legacy-ae4277f60d27ba40958547e368488ffb8.value: The political kingdom is distinct from a wider Luba cultural sphere. Only 1800 is curated before later-century fragmentation; founding myths, clan-based title succession and ethnic distribution do not define sovereign boundaries.

legacy-4e6c189275fdc6c0ed42ede65df3b4432.value: Multiethnic royal polity with tributary clients

legacy-fa9c3c8b05b507d3028726636b4536292.value: Lunda was a political state distinguished from culturally related peoples and Luba kingship. Only an early-century framework is accepted; sources differ over later fragmentation and no 1900 empire survival is asserted.

legacy-0ab7025c5dd4a04fdbdf92f265e3e9383.value: The source attests a sultanate developing royal trade power around 1800. Sabun individual accession is not assigned an exactday or year; Darfur kinship and historical influence do not establish present ownership.

legacy-19115554b47a37c4af9273a3ba45bed14.value: Highland royal polity alongside other Malagasy kingdoms

legacy-3296cfe58644af935dfc1ba34bcadd788.value: This early framework applies to the Merina polity. The generic Madagascar label in 1800 does not establish sole Merina sovereignty across the island. Contradictory named reign dates are omitted.

legacy-377e4232e3af0145678be44251e5fff68.value: Portuguese colonial footholds and administrative claims

legacy-c267b31d4af855c06de350ae977ce9ee1.value: The 1752 separation from Portuguese India established the Mozambique, Sofala and Rios de Sena administration. African polities persisted. Modern boundaries do not prove complete Portuguese rule; Delagoa Bay is not automatically equivalent to the whole administration.

legacy-d15e526125767e1afe91c8201bba0b44a.value: Changamire royal authority and regional subrulers

legacy-5e04dc7af3bc6d3b1d93f955ef4ff1eb1.value: The museum identifies Danangombe as the capital into the early 1800 s and Rozvi rulers into the 1830 s. This narrow 1800 core concerns a political state. Archaeological uncertainty and oral traditions do not establish exact lifetime dates.

legacy-2ebbb93b02470abbb3dca683bf4d30ffd.value: Representative Body with two chambers; five-member Executive Directory

legacy-5bc82fa31677c50038bc66af2990b1cd2.value: The Batavian Republic followed the overthrow of the earlier Dutch republic. Under the 1798 framework a five-member Executive Directory worked alongside a two-chamber Representative Body. Later changes established the Staatsbewind and then Schimmelpenninck’s Grand Pensionary government before the Kingdom of Holland in 1806.

legacy-c864920993ac8a204cf99e049437ca0fe.value: Electoral territory within the Holy Roman Empire

legacy-32a22af5b455117146c8bf499db40d384.value: Maximilian Joseph held the electoral title before assuming the royal title on 1 January 1806. This limited early profile does not project the later kingdom into 1800.

legacy-823aeef04b8eee067528a810be5022ff2.value: An overseas possession of the Portuguese monarchy, before the royal court transfer. A viceroyal snapshot label does not establish a named officeholder or exact territorial control.

legacy-f101d4c46d95ae6e215d63b854cdc972a.value: Imperial free city within the Holy Roman Empire

legacy-7b2f3929f2591180842fa1a9eed60b7be.value: Bremen’s archive distinguishes the imperial city from the fully sovereign Free State after the empire ended in 1806. The subsequent French annexation and restoration must not be bridged by a timeless city-state profile.

legacy-46a4628c2d5016cfcf44eecc36094a081.value: Rajah’s state with Company tribute obligations under treaty

legacy-b24695608323be95f75d2600c10772a46.value: Rajah retaining internal authority over the possessions specified in the treaty

legacy-e9fed9f0b3e6bcd9ee573d7aa89514866.value: The 1791 treaty specified tribute and internal authority under acknowledged Company sovereignty for recovered districts. Its territorial clauses are not flattened into a claim about every possession; the 1809 revision remains outside this dossier.

legacy-7fb2292c838be22dd83c21b05340b0b95.value: Royal government centred on Abomey palaces

legacy-ccc71bef59fdc2f9a2d9144aefdf293bd.value: Heritage chronology establishes political kingship; exact king and constitutional powers uncurated.

legacy-7e5c66de8200fd4664702886c0f1afb50.value: Composite monarchy under the Danish Crown

legacy-48cad363943f053f8bf7bd452aec621da.value: Norway belonged to the Danish composite monarchy before 1814. Frederik acted as regent during Christian VII’s reign and later became king. The Treaty of Kiel transferred Norway away from the Danish Crown; Norway’s constitutional movement and subsequent union with Sweden were separate developments.

legacy-d2916e37df78c93bc44af84324b8940d8.value: Nominal emperors and autonomous regional nobles

legacy-be58bacfbf75d0cc8274c827d25616444.value: Rival emperors and provincial military power preclude a unified effective central sovereignty.

legacy-54a670e6cc61e5a832f2498697981c196.value: First Consul and conservative Senate under the 1799 constitution

scope.description: Sourced national flag design of the selected historical state framework; no polygon-derived sovereignty or exact historical textile measurements.

qualifications: Schematic vector; no assertion of historically standardized RGB shades or universal military/merchant-ensign use.

legacy-2ddf981dc18b2a330e5325f6eab5b1fc5.value: The 1799 constitution placed Bonaparte in the office of First Consul and created a conservative Senate. This republican Consulate preceded the imperial transition in 1804; the same map label should not be read as an unchanged governmental form.

legacy-1623534ebe00e5724353884a38a2053cf.value: Nominal mek/sultan with dominant hereditary viziers

legacy-43de516a2e99d922afddd79fca628e801.value: After the 1761 coup the sultan was a figurehead; weakening vassal allegiance prevents projection of earlier peak central power.

legacy-520d893ffcede1ab946ec2392b138dc6a.value: Goa — Portuguese administration with British garrison

legacy-af7b24de5404ad55c897008ddaeb9a831.value: Portuguese colonial territory with British military presence

legacy-e64f04da335d14c07e0b3c652cc0ee561.value: Portuguese Governor-General and British garrison at strategic forts

legacy-ff54f90c728d15352df69e8e6b80d7c83.value: British troops arrived in September 1799 and remained until a withdrawal during 1815. A garrison’s presence does not automatically prove sovereign transfer. Curation stops before the uncertain withdrawal date.

legacy-b5392d1d51336e7af75a3e75b13a012e1.value: The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred the East India Company’s administrative powers, possessions and armed forces to the British Crown. Responsibility in Britain passed to a Secretary of State for India, while the Crown appointed the viceroy and governors. Later constitutional reforms changed the institutions within this imperial framework. This arrangement is commonly described as the British Raj. It was an imperial system, rather than an independent national government. The mapped entity should not be read as proof of uniform direct British administration across all of the subcontinent. Princely states had a distinct position, and the geographical dataset’s authority fields provide only a simplified representation. This dossier keeps that distinction visible rather than treating administrative control as an unqualified statement of sovereignty.

legacy-d974204abfaba0c3a960baff58eacca0a.value: The Meiji Constitution placed the emperor at the centre of the constitutional order. Its provisions described imperial sovereignty and provided for legislative power to be exercised with the Imperial Diet. The Diet consisted of a House of Peers and a House of Representatives. Ministers of state advised the emperor and bore responsibility for their advice. This dossier records those constitutional provisions rather than assuming that the formal document explains every aspect of political practice in the 1930s. Its curated coverage is limited to the imperial polity represented by the mapped identity. It does not use the post-war constitution or a modern government profile as a silent substitute for the selected historical period.

legacy-8ebe7b302643ebc26c8081c186e1b4d45.value: After Hitler’s appointment as chancellor in January 1933, the Nazi leadership dismantled Germany’s democratic institutions and suppressed political opposition. The regime used emergency powers and legislation to concentrate authority, while excluding opponents from public life. Following President Hindenburg’s death in August 1934, Hitler combined presidential authority with the chancellorship. The Nazi Party dominated a dictatorship rather than a competitive parliamentary system. This overview describes the consolidated regime of the mid-1930s, without treating its later territorial conquests as facts about every selected year. The atlas’s boundary reconstructions are a separate geographical source and do not establish the constitutional or political status of every territory represented on the map.

legacy-3dad9ec37f72c9211fdae9fbc85531f5b.value: The war in China that expanded in 1937 increasingly shaped Japan’s foreign relations. Japanese military operations and territorial ambitions brought escalating tension with the United States, which opposed the expansion of the conflict. At home, the Meiji Constitution continued to define imperial sovereignty and a bicameral Imperial Diet. Prime ministers changed repeatedly in 1939 and 1940; the dated cabinet records preserve those transitions. Prefectural census figures describe a narrower territory than the whole empire.

legacy-ea50d033e10c62c4c6a155f01fdc69e7b.value: George VI became king after Edward VIII’s abdication in December 1936. Chamberlain’s Conservative premiership began in May 1937. British policy sought to avoid another European war through negotiation and concessions; the Munich agreement of 1938 became its best-known expression. The monarch and prime minister held distinct offices within a parliamentary monarchy. The British Empire extended well beyond the United Kingdom’s domestic population series. This interval ends when Britain entered the war in September 1939.

legacy-b1a3dcc1a579926bfa0792426797faebc.value: Following his re-election in 1936, Franklin D. Roosevelt began a second presidential term on 20 January 1937, with John Nance Garner as vice-president. His first inauguration had taken place on 4 March 1933; the Twentieth Amendment changed the inauguration date for 1937 onward. Roosevelt communicated with the public through informal radio addresses. Early broadcasts discussed the banking crisis, the New Deal programme and economic recovery, followed by an address on public works and Social Security in 1935. His Good Neighbor Policy sought improved relations and trade with Latin America through a stated commitment to respect and non-intervention. The population figure shown separately is an earlier, geographically limited census observation, not a current-year estimate.

legacy-ad7f60e63ee383c179d36c070a2672a32.value: Churchill became prime minister in May 1940 and formed a wartime coalition. His Conservative affiliation should not be mistaken for the composition of that all-party administration. Britain’s war effort depended on military operations and cooperation with allies; the government continued to operate through parliamentary institutions. George VI remained monarch throughout the war. The leadership records preserve the change to Attlee in 1945 rather than assigning one prime minister to the entire transition year.

legacy-72c437f0aa2be162ba73c23297cdeb934.value: Attlee’s Labour government followed the 1945 election. Its programme expanded public services and nationalised important industries. The National Health Service and national insurance legislation were central to postwar reconstruction. Overseas, the government presided over independence for India and Pakistan and the end of British rule in other territories. These were changes in imperial relationships, not grounds for treating every formerly governed territory as a part of the United Kingdom’s domestic census population.
